source.title: Learning neuroimaging models from health system-scale data
source.authors: Yiwei Lyu; Samir Harake; A. Chowdury; Soumyanil Banerjee; Rachel Gologorsky; Shixuan Liu; Anna-Katharina Meissner; Akshay Rao; Chen-Hui Zhao; Akhil Kondepudi; Cheng Jiang; Xinhai Hou; Rushikesh S. Joshi; V. record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure content is flattened or difficult to read in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation perplexity for a radiology language model across report-data amounts, a limited test of the loss-versus-data part of V1. It does not fit or evaluate the claimed power law. Its image-model scaling results use downstream performance measures rather than held-out language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a validation-perplexity sweep for its neuroradiology language model and scaling results for Prima. Prima’s AUROC and retrieval results are included as related scaling findings, but they do not measure the loss or power-law form named by the claim versions. Other diagnosis, transfer, fairness, and architecture-ablation results are not rows for this claim.
record.test_reason: This is a neuroimaging foundation-model paper. Its scaling analyses are side checks of its own models, and the authors cite Kaplan et al. to read them. Validation perplexity of the GPT-2 radiology LM at 1%, 10% and 100% of reports (Ext. Data Fig. 3e) is the only held-out LM loss measure. It appears only as unreadable figure curves, with no fit, exponent, parameter or compute sweep, or token counts. Prima's data and compute sweeps measure downstream AUROC and retrieval accuracy of a vision-language model, not loss, and no power-law form or predictability fit is reported. No result can confirm or contradict any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors state that the radiology LM benefits from more report data. They state that Prima's performance improves consistently with more training data and compute, is non-saturating, and is consistent with neural scaling laws (citing Kaplan). From this they infer that more health-system data and compute will keep improving performance. They fit no power law and make no compute-optimal claims.
record.recipe_differences: The language-model result is a report-data percentage sweep tracking validation perplexity, rather than a systematic fit of loss against parameter count, token count, and compute. Prima’s reported scaling results use image-model diagnostic and retrieval performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The neuroradiology language-model validation perplexity is evaluated with different percentages of report data; Prima’s reported performance varies with training-data amount and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Prima's mean prospective diagnostic AUROC rises from 10% to 100% of UM220K studies (22K to 221K) with no saturation (Fig. 2c, Ext. Data Fig. 5g). Prospective top-1 retrieval accuracy keeps rising over 50 days, about 60 ExaFLOPs, of CLIP training (Ext. Data Fig. 6b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For a medical 3D vision-language model at fixed capacity, downstream diagnostic and retrieval performance increases monotonically with training data and training compute over the tested range, without saturation.

record.problems: The language-model scaling evidence is limited to validation perplexity over report-data percentages for one model. The paper does not provide a power-law fit, exponent, token counts, or parameter/compute sweep for that model. Prima’s scaling results are performance measures from figures and do not test the claimed language-model loss law.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. The numerous per-diagnosis and architecture-ablation results were not included because they do not report language-model loss scaling or the same power-law measure.

untested.parts: Power-law form, parameter and compute scaling, and readable loss values over several orders of magnitude are all untested. Only a three-point data-fraction perplexity curve exists, shown as a figure.
All parts: no extrapolation from small-run fits.
All parts: architecture ablations change design (flat ViT, CNN) without holding parameter count fixed, and are measured by AUROC.
Power-law form for imaging or vision-language loss is untested. Only monotone downstream gains are shown.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss is untested. Only monotone, non-saturating improvement is shown.
All parts: no fitting choices or exponents compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label is removed. It rested on untested parts (no fit, no parameter or compute sweep), which belong under untested, not limits_scope. All V1-linked rows are cannot_determine, so no verdict can be given. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies report-data percentage for one neuroradiology language model, but does not report parameter-count or compute scaling, token counts, a fitted power-law form or exponent, or evidence spanning several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is evaluated against much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count is reported for language-model loss.
Prima is an imaging model and its data/compute scaling results concern AUROC and retrieval, not whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in another modality or training regime.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but the paper does not test whether their performance is predictably related to pretraining loss or scale.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, or evidence of curves bending away from a fitted power law, is reported.

rows.check: Downstream AUROC of an imaging VLM at 10-100% of UM220K, a range of only one order of magnitude. This is not pretraining loss and not a predictability fit, so it belongs under fits_no_version.
